# Laundry Room Ventilation

## Overview

The laundry room is a lean-to off the kitchen, built from single skin block, and it has always run damp. In winter the small window fogs on the inside within ten minutes of a wash and the cold outer wall beads with moisture down to the skirting. I left it for two winters before I worked out that the room was breathing nothing but its own wet air. A load of washing adds several litres of water vapour to a room this size, and with the door shut and no path out, that vapour lands on the first cold surface it meets. The window frame went soft at the bottom corner and I had to dig out and replace a length of beading, which cost me a Saturday and a tin of filler. That was the year I decided the room needed a proper path for the air, not another coat of bathroom paint. The room is small, about two metres by one and a half with a ceiling at 2.2 m, so there is very little air in it to absorb the vapour a wash gives off.

## Setup

I fitted a wall extractor rated at 15 litres a second, which is more than the four air changes an hour a room this size really needs, but I wanted headroom for a wet day. The fan sits high on the wall opposite the window, so it pulls air across the room and past the washing before it leaves. The duct is 100 mm flexible run up through the loft, roughly 3 m of it, with a condensation trap at the low point and an external flap on the gable. The trap matters because warm wet air cools as it climbs into the loft and drops water back down the pipe; the trap catches that and drains it out through the wall. I lagged the last metre of duct in the loft with a foil wrap so the air reaches the flap still warm. The trickle vents above the window stay open all year, both of them, giving the fan a path to pull fresh air in behind it. The target is to keep the room under 55% relative humidity, which is where the meter on the shelf sits on a normal day. On a wash day it will climb to 70% and then fall back once the fan has run its spell. The fan is on a run-on timer set to 20 minutes, wired to the light switch so nobody has to remember it.

## Maintenance

The extractor grille collects fluff and gets a wipe and a brush every quarter, which takes five minutes with the cover unclipped. A gentle vacuum over the blades is enough; I never run water through the unit itself. The grille lifts away for a rinse in warm water if the fibre has gone stiff, and it goes back once it is bone dry. In spring I climb the ladder on the gable end and clear the external flap of nests, because the starlings find it a sheltered spot and will fill it with straw in a fortnight. The flap has to swing freely on its hinge or the whole duct is just a hole in the wall. I check the duct joints in the loft at the same time, pushing each collar home and taping any that have worked loose, since a joint that has slipped apart dumps wet air straight into the roof space. The trap gets emptied and rinsed when I am up there anyway, and I pour a mug of water through it to prove it still drains. Once a year I brush the duct run itself with a pull-through, working from the gable end back towards the fan.

## Notes

The door stays shut while the fan runs, otherwise the fan pulls its air from the kitchen and the wet air in here just sits. After a load I leave the fan running for another 20 minutes to clear the last of the vapour, and I crack the window for that spell in summer. The humidity meter lives on the wall by the door so I can see at a glance whether the room is drying out or holding water. I run the fan at the low speed on ordinary days and the boost only after a wash. The trickle vents stay open even in a cold snap, because a room sealed up tight holds its moisture longer than one with a slow, steady draught. In summer I leave the window on the latch all day and the fan does very little, and in winter the reverse is true and the fan does the work. The meter tells me which way to run it without my having to guess.
